title: Why On-Site AI Shopping Assistants Give Wrong Answers
summary: On-site AI shopping assistants give wrong answers when product data is messy, inaccurate or missing. Here is how to find and fix the gaps in your catalog.
body_markdown:
AI shopping assistants give wrong answers for many reasons. Some, such as hallucination or vague and confusing questions from shoppers, are hard to control and not productive to chase. The biggest reason, and the one a team can fix, is the underlying product data. When product data is messy, inaccurate or missing, the assistant will give wrong answers.


This article is about the assistant on a company's own storefront: the virtual shopping assistant that shoppers chat with on your site, not ChatGPT, Google AI Mode or other external shopping agents.


The sections below explain how on-site assistants use product data. They then set out a practical process that ecommerce brands, retailers and distributors can use to improve AI shopping assistant accuracy at the source.


## How do AI shopping assistants work?


An AI shopping assistant is a conversational tool on an online store that answers product questions and recommends items in response to plain-language requests. To answer well, it needs facts about the products. On a store's own site, the most reliable place for those facts is the product catalog.


To use the catalog, the assistant first looks up the products and details that match the shopper's question, then passes them to a large language model. The model writes its reply from those facts rather than from what it learned in training alone. NVIDIA's retail shopping advisor workflow, for example, is designed to[answer shoppers' questions from a company's product catalog](https://catalog.ngc.nvidia.com/orgs/nvidia/teams/aiworkflows/collections/retail_shopping_advisor) .


The process works in four steps:


1. **Store the catalog.** Product titles, descriptions, attributes and other content are converted into embeddings, which are numerical representations of meaning, and saved in a database built for searching by meaning. This stored copy of the catalog is what the assistant draws on.
2. **Find matching products.** The shopper's question is converted into an embedding too, and the system compares it with the stored ones to find the closest products and passages.
3. **Add the facts to the question.** The system places the product data it found alongside the shopper's question, so the model sees both together.
4. **Write the answer.** The model writes a reply from the question and the product data in front of it.


The stored copy has to keep pace with the catalog. When a price, stock level or specification changes, the copy needs updating too, or the assistant keeps answering from the old value.


Matching by meaning is not the only way to find products. An assistant can also filter on structured fields such as material, fit or price. A filter can only include a product when that field exists and holds a correct value.


The last safeguard is grounding, which ties each answer to the source data behind it. Grounding lowers the chance that a model invents content. In NVIDIA's reference, a grounding step keeps each reply to the facts in the catalog. A grounded assistant repeats what the catalog says, so a wrong or empty field becomes a wrong or empty answer.


## Why do AI shopping assistants give wrong answers?


An assistant gives wrong answers when the model guesses or when the product data it retrieves is missing, wrong, inconsistent, miscategorized or out of date.


### The model guesses when it lacks an answer


Research from OpenAI shows that large language models[sometimes guess when they are uncertain, producing statements that sound plausible but are wrong](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.04664) .


Prompting reduces the problem but does not remove it. Techniques such as letting the model admit uncertainty or limiting it to supplied documents cut hallucinations without eliminating them. Model behavior sits mostly with the assistant's vendor. For a catalog team, the useful point is that every missing value gives the model another gap to guess into.


### Attributes are missing


When a shopper asks whether a backpack fits a 16-inch laptop, the assistant needs a laptop compartment size in the data. If the field is blank, or the schema has no such field, retrieval has nothing to return. A filter on that attribute also leaves the product out.


### Values are wrong or contradict each other


A title that says 18V next to a voltage field that says 20V gives the assistant two answers. A grounded assistant repeats catalog facts, so it can state the wrong one with confidence. Wrong values can enter through supplier feeds, copied listings or outdated spec sheets.


Terminology adds to the problem. Language models can give inaccurate responses when sources use the same term for different things. Inside one catalog, the same thing happens when two suppliers use one word for different measurements, such as length meaning the product in one feed and the package in another.


### Values and names are inconsistent


The same color might appear as navy, Navy Blue and NVY, or the same measurement in centimeters in one record and inches in another. A structured filter for navy then returns only part of the range.


### Products sit in the wrong category


The category decides which attributes a product carries. In Shopify, for example, category metafields map to specific categories in its Standard Product Taxonomy, so a product in the shirts category gets fields for neckline and fabric. A shirt filed under a generic category misses those fields and drops out of answers that filter by category.


### Data is out of date


Prices, stock levels and specifications change. The assistant answers from its stored copy of the catalog, so its answers are only as current as that copy's last update. An assistant reading last week's stock file will recommend products that are no longer available.


## How do you fix wrong answers from an AI shopping assistant?


The fixes follow a sequence. Find what is missing and fill it, check the values already there, put products in the right categories, then test. Each step works for ecommerce brands, retailers and distributors, whether the catalog holds hundreds or millions of SKUs.


### Find missing attributes from what shoppers ask


Start with a schema audit. For each category, list every attribute, mark it required or optional, and record its fill rate across products. This shows blank fields, but only for attributes you have already defined. It does not reveal details shoppers need that your schema never captured.


To find those, collect the questions shoppers ask in their own words from these sources:


- **On-site search terms.** In Google Analytics 4, enhanced measurement[records each search results view along with the search term](https://support.google.com/analytics/answer/9216061?hl=en) . On Shopify, the searches with no results report[breaks down the terms customers used to search for products](https://help.shopify.com/en/manual/reports-and-analytics/shopify-reports/report-types/default-reports/behaviour-reports) that returned nothing.
- **Assistant conversation logs.** Export the prompts shoppers send to the assistant. Prioritize questions that got no answer, a hedged answer or a rephrased follow-up.
- **Support tickets and pre-sale chats.** Product questions that reach customer service, such as whether an item is dishwasher safe, point to details the product page did not answer.


Then map those questions to attributes:


1. Pull three to six months of search terms, prompts and support questions, grouped by product category.
2. Break each one into the constraints it contains. "Waterproof hiking boots for wide feet under $150" contains waterproofing, activity, width and price.
3. Match each constraint to an attribute in your schema. Mark it "no attribute" when nothing fits.
4. Count how often each attribute is requested per category.
5. Sort the results into three groups: not in the schema, in the schema but poorly filled, and filled but still producing wrong answers.
6. Rank the gaps by request volume and the number of products affected.


A simple gap table keeps the work focused:


Category Shopper constraint Attribute In schema? Fill rate Requests


Hiking boots wide feet Width fit No n/a High


Hiking boots waterproof Waterproofing Yes Low High


Backpacks fits 16-inch laptop Laptop compartment size Yes Medium Medium


### Fill missing attributes and values


If an attribute is not in the schema, add it to the category where it belongs. Define its name, data type, unit and allowed values before anyone fills it. Agreeing on allowed values first prevents the inconsistency problems described above.


If the attribute exists but is empty, fill it from the most reliable source available. Supplier data and manufacturer spec sheets come first, followed by manufacturer product pages. Product images hold data too, such as color, material and style.


AI can enrich a catalog at scale when it works inside written guidelines. Set these before you run it:


- **Allowed values.** List the accepted values and units for each attribute so output stays consistent.
- **Source priority.** Decide which sources to prioritize when they disagree, such as the manufacturer over a reseller.
- **Blank over guess.** Leave a field empty and flag it when no source supports a value.
- **Human review.** Have a reviewer check a sample from every batch, plus every flagged value, before publishing.


Hypotenuse AI's[AI product data enrichment](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/features/ecommerce-product-data-enrichment) fills missing attributes from the web, UPCs, images and spec sheets. Every value it fills shows where it came from, and your team reviews values before anything is published. For generated product copy, teams can set rules for brand words, banned phrases and restricted language so descriptions stay in their[brand voice](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/features/brand-voice) .


### Check product data for inaccurate values


Check existing values against the manufacturer, since a grounded assistant repeats whatever the catalog says. The manufacturer's product page or spec sheet is the most reliable reference, followed by supplier data and other reliable web sources.


Start with the attributes shoppers ask about most and the products with the most traffic. Confirm each value against the outside source, correct it when it differs, and record the source you used. When sources disagree, follow the source priority you set for enrichment.


Normalize values in the same pass. Map variants such as Navy Blue and NVY to one allowed value, and convert each attribute to a single unit.


### Fix categorization with a standard taxonomy


There is no need to design a taxonomy from scratch. Two public taxonomies give a strong starting point:


- **Google product taxonomy.** It is a[category tree that Google uses to sort products for Google Shopping](https://support.google.com/merchants/answer/6324436) , running from broad to specific levels such as Electronics > Communications > Telephony > Mobile Phones. The full list can be downloaded as a spreadsheet or a plain-text file.
- **Shopify Standard Product Taxonomy.** It is an[open-source, global product classification made up of categories, attributes and attribute values](https://shopify.github.io/product-taxonomy/) . The taxonomy's GitHub repository is released under the MIT License and includes a mapping to Google's taxonomy.


Adapt the standard to your range. Remove branches you do not sell, split categories where your range is deep, and rename labels to match the words shoppers use in search. Attach a defined attribute set to each leaf category, and keep a mapping back to the standard so channel feeds stay correct.


Then recategorize existing products and check that items of the same type land in the same leaf category.[AI product categorization](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/features/ai-product-categorization) from Hypotenuse AI places every SKU in the right category of your own taxonomy in bulk, however deep the category tree goes.


### Keep one source of product data in sync


The assistant should read from the same product record as your product pages, site search and channel feeds, so a fix made once shows up everywhere. Teams without an existing PIM can use an[AI PIM](https://www.hypotenuse.ai/features/ai-pim-solution) such as Hypotenuse AI as their single source of truth for product data.


Match the refresh schedule to how fast each field changes. The assistant reads a stored copy of the catalog, so stock and price need near real-time updates, while specifications can follow a batch schedule.


### Test the assistant with real shopper questions


Turn the question list from your attribute audit into a test set, with the correct answer for each question taken from the verified product record. Include compatibility, stock and specification questions, since those depend on exact values. Rerun the set after each data fix to see which answers improved and which gaps remain.


## Frequently asked questions


### What does an AI shopping assistant do?


An AI shopping assistant helps shoppers find and choose products through conversation. It answers questions about specifications, sizing, compatibility and availability, and recommends items that match what the shopper describes. On a store's own site, it draws those answers from the store's product catalog.


### Is an AI assistant the same as a chatbot?


Not quite. A traditional chatbot follows scripted flows or answers a fixed set of questions, often about orders, shipping and returns. An AI shopping assistant uses a language model to interpret open-ended requests, retrieve matching products and answer follow-up questions about them. Because its answers are about products, it depends far more on product data.


### What should I do if my AI gives a wrong answer?


For a storefront assistant, treat each wrong answer as a data ticket. Log the question and the answer, then check what the assistant retrieved. If the right product came back with a missing or wrong value, fix the product record. If the wrong products came back, check categories and attribute values. Add the question to your test set so the fix stays verified.


## Improve AI shopping assistant accuracy at the source


An on-site assistant answers from the product data it retrieves, so its accuracy rises as the catalog improves. Start with the attributes shoppers ask about most and work outward from there.
